paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: when fear shows up, Jacob does BOTH. He makes a plan, and he prays. He splits his people into two camps and picks out a gift, and in between he talks to God (Genesis 32:7-8, 13). I think that's the whole lesson. Planning isn't the problem. Planning with no prayer would be the problem.

Now look at what he says in that prayer. He tells God, "I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant." Then he asks, "Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau," and he holds up what God told him: "I will surely make you prosper" (Genesis 32:10-12). He doesn't bring God his record. He brings God's own words. Honest and humble, with the promise in both hands, and that's how you pray when you're scared.

And here's the part that hits home. Jacob is still hoping the gifts will do the work, saying "perhaps he will accept me" (Genesis 32:20). That's a very human thing to do, because we all send a few gifts ahead and hope. The story isn't over, and Jacob still has a long night coming. But you can pray like Jacob did, with a real plan in one hand and God's promise in the other.
